neuter, neutra, neutrum

pronoun and adjective; gen. neutrīus, dat. neutrī · Declension on Wiktionary

neither (of two)

With a genitive of the pair: neutrum eōrum, neither of them. Of more than two, “none” is nūllus (see none). “Neither … nor” is nec … nec.

Examples

  • Leporēs duo quī īnsequitur, is neutrum capit.

    Whoever chases two hares catches neither.Ps.-Publil. L 3

  • Ad duo festīnāns neutrum bene perēgeris.

    Rush at two things and you’ll finish neither well.Ps.-Publil. A 5

  • ita fīet, ut, cum aequālī cūrā linguam utramque tuērī coeperīmus, neutra alterī officiat

    so it will come about that, once we begin to look after both languages with equal care, neither will get in the way of the otherQuint. 1.1.14

  • aliōquī neutrum sine alterō sufficit

    otherwise neither is enough without the otherQuint. 2.9.3

  • dēbēmus neutrum eōrum contrā alium juvāre

    we ought to help neither of them against the otherCaes. BC 1.35.5 (Lewis & Short)

  • Neutrum vērō.

    Actually, neither.Traupman 68

See also either, both, none.

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-publilius, loci-quintilianus), checked against the editions named there.

Publilius is cited as the loci collection numbers him, by position under each initial letter in the Latin Library text; from N onwards that numbering differs from Meyer’s. “Ps.-Publil.” marks lines from the later collections printed with him.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
